newsitem.title: UK: Direct Line slams lenders on home insurance.
newsitem.headline: Direct Line slams lenders on home insurance.

text.p: Britain's leading direct insurer accused rival banks and building societies on Tuesday of "restrictive practices" in the home insurance market and called for new legislation to decouple policies from home loans.

Royal Bank of Scotland's insurance subsidiary Direct Line accused middlemen, and principally mortgage providers, of extracting 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) in commission last year from customers spending 5.25 billion on household cover. Banks and building societies took 720 million pounds in commission.
Ninety percent of the 23 million owner-occupied households in the UK are insured. Banks and building societies have the largest share, accounting for 42 percent of all home insurance.
In a report drawing on research from stockbroker Gerrard Vivian Gray, Direct Line said customers were paying more than they needed to.

It said that mortgage providers like banks and building societies were seeking to strengthen their grip on underwriting to protect profits in the competitive lending market. Many of the larger institutions already limit business to one insurer.

"They continue to dominate the market and restrict customer choice simply by using their proximity at the point of mortgage sale to their advantage by selling costly insurance policies, often tied to mortgages," said Direct Line's chief executive Ian Chippendale in a statement accompanying the report.
The report said the strength of the mortgage providers was rooted in "structure" insurance, a condition imposed by lenders to obtain security should the mortgaged property be damaged.

Direct Line, which pioneered the sale of motor insurance over the telephone and has sold 800,000 policies in the home insurance market where direct sales account for just three percent of the total, began a campaign six years ago against what it called "building societies' restrictive practices".

In June 1994, the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) concluded that relevant legislation addressing freedom of choice and the link between home insurance and mortgages should be implemented immediately. Building societies would have had to disclose more information about their packaged products. But nothing happened.

"More than two years later, there has been little, if any, progress made towards implementation," said Direct Line. "The majority of customers are still paying over the odds...Banks and building societies continue to restrict customer choice."

Despite this, policyholders who choose to shop around will find they can pay less for household cover than they would have a couple of years ago. Premiums in much of the insurance market have fallen amid intense competition between insurance providers, some of it spurred on by the arrival of direct sellers.

This was highlighted by news on Monday that U.S. insurer St Paul International is to seek more imaginative ways to increase its market share, announcing plans to offer more competitive terms on household policies to older, well-heeled customers.
